name: congenital fibrosis of extraocular muscles
aliases: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles

reference.source: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
clinicalPearls: A congenital, non-progressive restrictive ophthalmoplegia now recognised as a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder affecting the oculomotor (III) nerve and nucleus, sometimes with trochlear (IV) involvement
Classic presentation is bilateral ptosis with the eyes fixed in a downward (infraducted) position and a compensatory chin-up head posture to see
Because the globes are tethered below the horizontal midline, patients characteristically make upward eye movements to fixate and have marked limitation of elevation
Forced duction testing is positive owing to secondary fibrosis of the extraocular muscles, which follows the primary dysinnervation rather than being the initial lesion

Recognised subtypes include CFEOM1 (KIF21A, classic bilateral, autosomal dominant), CFEOM2 (PHOX2A/ARIX, autosomal recessive, more complete external ophthalmoplegia) and CFEOM3 (TUBB3, variable severity, sometimes autosomal dominant)
TUBB3-related (CFEOM3) disease may carry additional features such as peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay, facial weakness and brain malformations
Amblyopia is common from ptosis, strabismus and refractive error, and aberrant regeneration with lid or globe synkinesis may be seen
Surgery is challenging, requiring large recessions of tight muscles and cautious ptosis repair given poor elevation and a deficient Bell's phenomenon
reference.pathophysiology: CFEOM is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder caused by abnormal development of the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and their nerves, producing primary dysinnervation of the extraocular muscles, particularly the superior division of the third nerve supplying the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris. Secondary fibrosis and abnormal muscle development follow the aberrant innervation. Identified genes disrupt axon guidance and neuronal development: KIF21A, a kinesin motor for anterograde axonal transport, in CFEOM1; PHOX2A, a transcription factor required for oculomotor and trochlear nucleus development, in CFEOM2; and TUBB3, a neuron-specific beta-tubulin, in CFEOM3. The result is a congenital, non-progressive restrictive ophthalmoplegia with ptosis.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (mitochondrial), which is progressive and later in onset
Congenital and juvenile myasthenia gravis and congenital myasthenic syndromes
Mobius syndrome and other congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders (Duane, monocular elevation deficiency)
Congenital myopathies (for example centronuclear) with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis
Thyroid eye disease with restrictive myopathy in older patients
Blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome for the ptosis component
additionalInvestigations: Forced duction testing to confirm restriction
Orthoptic measurement of ductions, ocular alignment and compensatory head posture
Genetic testing for KIF21A, PHOX2A and TUBB3, with a CFEOM panel or exome if needed
MRI of the orbits and brain to assess extraocular muscle bulk and cranial nerve/brainstem development
Family assessment and pedigree, given autosomal dominant inheritance in CFEOM1 and CFEOM3
Assessment for associated neurological features when TUBB3-related disease is suspected
redFlags: Corneal exposure after ptosis surgery given poor elevation and a deficient Bell's phenomenon
A progressive rather than static course, prompting reconsideration of CPEO or myasthenia
Associated neurological deterioration suggesting a TUBB3 tubulinopathy phenotype
Dense amblyopia in the visually immature child
reference.prognosis: The condition is congenital and non-progressive, and visual and functional outcomes depend chiefly on amblyopia management and carefully staged strabismus and ptosis surgery. Ocular motility rarely normalises, but head posture, alignment and lid position can be meaningfully improved surgically.
pitfalls: Undertaking standard ptosis repair without recognising poor elevation and Bell's phenomenon, risking exposure keratopathy
Mistaking the restrictive limitation for a simple third nerve palsy or myasthenia
Missing amblyopia while focusing on the motility defect
Not testing for TUBB3-associated systemic and neurological features
Underestimating the tightness of the muscles at surgery despite positive forced ductions
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: There is no medical therapy; carefully staged strabismus surgery with large recessions of the tethered muscles is used to improve primary-position alignment and correct the compensatory chin-up head posture
Undertake ptosis correction, usually frontalis suspension, to open the visual axis while guarding against corneal exposure given defective elevation and poor Bell's phenomenon
Aggressively manage amblyopia with refractive correction and occlusion to maximise vision in early childhood
Protect the ocular surface with lubrication following lid surgery to prevent exposure keratopathy
Screen for the extra-ocular features of TUBB3-related disease such as peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay, facial weakness and brain malformation, involving neurology as needed
Offer genetic counselling and pedigree assessment for the KIF21A, PHOX2A and TUBB3 subtypes, coordinating paediatric ophthalmology, orthoptics and clinical genetics
